To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) glutaminase activity is regulated by the availability of ammonia in the extracellular environment; (2) ammonia and glutamine stabilize the enzyme and induce its activity in primary cultures; (3) in hepatocyte cultures ammonia and glutamine are required to maintain the enzyme activity, and the inactivation of glutamine activity in vivo under certain circumstances may be due to the lack of ammonia in the environment.

the loss of glutaminase from cultured rat hepatocytes in the absence of NH3 is prevented by the presence of high concentrations of glutamate and/or glutamine in the culture medium and that the induction of glutaminases by glucagon is dependent on the presence of NH3.
glutamine, ammonia, and glucagon regulate the long-term stability and the induction of phosphate-dependent glutamine in hepatocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long-term regulation (24-40 h) of the phosphate-dependent glutaminases activity in primary cultures hepatocytes.
the role of ammonia in the control of glutaminase and urea-cycle enzyme activities.
the regulation of glutaminase, a key enzyme in glutamine catabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

glutaminase activity is regulated at the level of enzyme synthesis, and that the synthesis of the enzyme is regulated by the availability of ammonia and glutamine, which may be important for the maintenance of the intracellular glutamine pool.
the loss of activity was not due to a loss of enzyme protein, but to a change in the enzyme conformation or to the presence of an inhibitory factor.
the in vitro loss of glutaminase and the in vivo loss of glutaminases in liver are due to a deficiency of ammonia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NH3 and high concentrations of glutamate and glutamine in the medium are essential for the maintenance and induction of phosphate-dependent glutamine activity in rat hepatocytes.

the inactivation of glutamine synthetase and glutaminase in liver cells is due to lack of ammonia in the extracellular environment, whereas the induction of both enzymes is dependent on the presence of both glutamine and ammonia.

the inactivation of glutamine-dependent phosphate-dependent glutaminases in hepatocytes and other tissues is due to a lack of ammonia and/or high concentrations of glutaminase, and that the inactivation is prevented by the continuous presence in culture of high concentrations of glutamate and ammonia.
The main takeaway from our work is that

ammonia and glutamine are necessary for the long-term regulation and stabilization of glutaminase, and that inactivation of glutamine may occur under certain conditions due to the lack of NH3 and glutamate in the extracellular environment.
glutamine is an essential component for the long-term regulation and stabilization of glutaminase.
the loss of glutamine in hepatocytes is not due to the loss of enzyme activity.
